i

1I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 134
i OurBigBook.com
Lagrange theorem for polynomial congruences says that a nonzero polynomial of degree d over a field has at most d distinct roots of a polynomial. It follows by repeatedly factoring out x−a at a root. Over the finite field Fp​, the only solutions of x2=1 are 1 and −1: these are distinct because p is odd, and the root bound excludes any others.
Every nonzero element has a unique multiplicative inverse. Pair each element of Fp×​ with its inverse. All pairs of distinct elements contribute 1 to the product; the only unpaired elements are 1 and −1. Thus Wilson theorem follows:
(p−1)!≡−1(modp).​
(1)
If Lagrange's theorem is formulated for finite groups, it states that the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group; in particular every element of Fp×​ has order dividing p−1. The inverse-pairing proof above establishes the required congruence directly.

Put m=(p−1)/2 and let O=1⋅3⋅5⋯(p−2). The even residues 2,4,…,p−1 are precisely the negatives, in reverse order, of the odd residues 1,3,…,p−2. Hence their product is (−1)mO in the finite field Fp​. Applying Wilson theorem gives
−1≡(p−1)!=O((−1)mO)=(−1)mO2(modp).
(2)
The initial factor 12 can be omitted, so
32⋅52⋯(p−2)2≡(−1)m+1=(−1)(p+1)/2(modp).​
(3)
For p=3 the product is empty and equals 1, consistently with the formula.

3G (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 131
3G OurBigBook.com
A Kleinian group is a discrete subgroup of PSL2​(C), acting by Möbius transformations on the Riemann sphere, equivalently by orientation-preserving isometries of hyperbolic space H3.
Consider the classes of
A=(10​21​),B=(12​01​).
(10)
They generate a discrete subgroup because their matrix representatives have integer entries: a sequence of such matrices converging to I or −I is eventually constant. On the real projective line set X={x:∣x∣>1}∪{∞} and Y={x:∣x∣<1}. For every nonzero integer m,
Am(x)=x+2m,Bm(x)=2mx+1x​,Am(Y)⊂X,Bm(X)⊂Y.
(11)
The last inclusion follows from ∣2mx+1∣≥2∣x∣−1>∣x∣ when ∣x∣>1; also Bm(∞)=1/(2m)∈Y. The ping-pong lemma therefore says that the subgroup is the free product ⟨A⟩∗⟨B⟩. Both generators have infinite order, so
⟨A,B⟩≅Z∗Z,​
(12)
a free group on two generators. The ping-pong inclusions ensure that no nonempty reduced word can act as the identity, which is the essential freeness argument.

For a binary linear code C≤F2n​, its rank is its dimension of a vector space r. Use the weight enumerator convention
WC​(s,t)=∑c∈C​sw(c)tn−w(c),
(13)
where w(c) is the Hamming weight. This convention is essential here: WC​(1,0) counts words of weight n, rather than zero words. There are 2r codewords, so WC​(1,1)=2r​.
There is only one binary word of weight n, namely 1=(1,…,1). Thus WC​(1,0)=1 precisely when 1∈C. If this holds, the linear map c↦c+1 is a bijection of C and replaces weight w by n−w; hence WC​(s,t)=WC​(t,s). Conversely this symmetry gives WC​(1,0)=WC​(0,1)=1, because the zero word is the unique word of weight zero.
The repetition code consists of 0,1, giving
Wrep​(s,t)=tn+sn.​
(14)
The single parity-check code consists of all words of even weight. Exactly (jn​) words have weight j, so the binomial theorem gives
Wparity​(s,t)=j even∑​(jn​)sjtn−j=2(t+s)n+(t−s)n​.​
(15)

A generalized linear model has independent responses whose distributions belong to an exponential family:
fi​(yi​;θi​,ϕ)=exp{ai​(ϕ)yi​θi​−b(θi​)​+ci​(yi​,ϕ)}.
(16)
Here the expected value and variance are μi​=b′(θi​) and Var(Yi​)=ai​(ϕ)b′′(θi​). A specified one-to-one link function g connects the mean to the linear predictor: g(μi​)=xiT​β. The canonical link function is g(μi​)=θi​.
In binomial regression, Yi​∼Bin(mi​,pi​) independently, with known trial counts mi​ and probabilities related to the predictor. The logistic regression and probit regression specifications are respectively
log1−pi​pi​​=xiT​β,pi​=1+exiT​βexiT​β​;Φ−1(pi​)=xiT​β,pi​=Φ(xiT​β).​
(17)
Here Φ is the standard normal distribution function. The binomial log-density contains yi​log(pi​/(1−pi​))+mi​log(1−pi​), so its natural parameter is the log-odds: the logistic link is canonical. If the response mean is written as μi​=mi​pi​, the canonical link is gi​(μi​)=log(μi​/(mi​−μi​)).

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 179 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 179
6B OurBigBook.com
The physical state space is the positively invariant set X,Y,Z≥0, X+Y+Z=N: adding the equations gives zero, and the vector field points inward at each coordinate boundary. At an equilibrium point, either Y=0, giving (X,Y,Z)=(N,0,0), or βX=b+r. Therefore
Nc​=βb+r​,Xs​=Nc​,Ys​=b+rb(N−Nc​)​,Zs​=b+rr(N−Nc​)​.​
(18)
A positive endemic equilibrium exists exactly when N>Nc​.
For N<Nc​, put d=b+r−βN>0. Since X≤N,
Y˙≤−dY,0≤Y(t)≤Y(0)e−dt,Z(t)=Z(0)e−bt+r∫0t​e−b(t−s)Y(s)ds⟶0.
(19)
The last limit follows either by evaluating the exponential integral (with a te−bt term when d=b), or by splitting it into an early decaying part and a late part with uniformly small Y. Hence X→N for every physical initial condition. Although immune numbers need not decrease monotonically initially, both infected and immune numbers tend to zero.
At the endemic equilibrium, the Jacobian matrix of the X,Y subsystem is
J=(−b−βYs​βYs​​−βXs​0​).
(20)
A disturbance proportional to ept therefore obeys
p2+(b+βYs​)p+β2Xs​Ys​=0.​
(21)
Both coefficients are positive. Real roots have negative sum and positive product; complex conjugate roots have real part −(b+βYs​)/2<0. Thus the endemic equilibrium is asymptotically stable by linear stability analysis.

i OurBigBook.com
For the iteration of a map f(x)=λx(1−x2), a fixed point satisfies x[1−λ+λx2]=0. If 0<λ<1, the bracket is strictly positive, so the sole fixed point is 0. Its multiplier of a periodic orbit of an iteration is f′(0)=λ, whose modulus is below one. Thus x=0 is locally asymptotically stable​ by fixed point stability for an iteration.

Using fixed point stability for an iteration, ∣3−2λ∣<1 exactly when 1<λ<2, and ∣3−2λ∣>1 when λ>2. Hence
x±​ stable for 1<λ<2,unstable for λ>2.​

The numbers zj​ are the nonzero zeros of a function f, repeated according to their multiplicity. The displayed Weierstrass factorization theorem formula uses genus-one Weierstrass elementary factors and a linear exponential factor; it applies under the corresponding growth assumptions, rather than to every arbitrary entire function.
Apply it to the entire function g(z)=sin(πz)/(πz), with its removable value g(0)=1. Its zeros are ±1,±2,…, each simple, and g′(0)=0 because g is even. Pairing the factors at n and −n gives
(1−z/n)ez/n(1+z/n)e−z/n=1−z2/n2,
(27)
so
πzsin(πz)​=n=1∏∞​(1−n2z2​).​
(28)
The product converges uniformly on compact subsets because ∑n−2<∞. Away from the integers its logarithmic derivative can be taken term by term: the resulting series also converges locally uniformly, its terms being O(n−2). Hence
πcot(πz)−z1​=∑n=1∞​1−z2/n2−2z/n2​,πcot(πz)=z1​+2n=1∑∞​z2−n2z​.​
(29)
This is an identity of meromorphic functions, understood away from their poles.

Noether theorem associates a conserved quantity ∑i​pi​δqi​ to a continuous symmetry of the Lagrangian (with the usual boundary-term correction if the Lagrangian changes by a total derivative). The angles ψ and ϕ are cyclic coordinates, so for the heavy symmetric top
pψ​=I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ)=b,pϕ​=I1​ϕ˙​sin2θ+bcosθ=a.​
(30)
Time-translation symmetry gives conserved energy, whose Hamiltonian expression is
E=2I1​pθ2​​+2I1​sin2θ(pϕ​−pψ​cosθ)2​+2I3​pψ2​​+Mglcosθ.​
(31)
It is quadratic in the momenta; pθ​=I1​θ˙. Eliminating the cyclic velocities and putting μ=cosθ, so μ˙​2=sin2θθ˙2, yields
μ˙​2=I1​2​(1−μ2)(E−2I3​b2​−Mglμ)−I12​(a−bμ)2​=F(μ).​
(32)
The first term has degree three and the second degree two, displaying the cubic governing nutation.

Electrical neutrality gives ne​≃np​ at the accuracy of the proposed estimate. With V∼R3 and np​∼M/(mp​R3), the degenerate electron gas result gives
Ekin​∼hc(mp​M​)4/3R1​.​
(36)
The gravitational potential energy is Egrav​∼−GM2/R. Both scale as R−1, so in the strictly ultrarelativistic approximation
Etotal​∼R1​[hc(mp​M​)4/3−GM2].
(37)
For sufficiently large mass the bracket is negative, and contraction lowers the energy without bound in this model: electron degeneracy pressure cannot halt collapse. Equating the scales gives the Chandrasekhar mass
Mcrit​∼mp2​(hc/G)3/2​.​
(38)
Below this scale, the strictly ultrarelativistic expression alone has no finite-radius energy minimum; including the transition to nonrelativistic electrons produces the stable white dwarf branch. Composition and the stellar density profile supply the numerical factors omitted by this scaling estimate.

For σ=Res>1, the Dirichlet series ζ(s)=∑n≥1​n−s is absolutely convergent. A finite product over primes p≤P can be expanded into absolutely convergent geometric series. By unique prime factorization,
∏p≤P​(1−p−s)−1=∑n≥1all prime factors of n≤P​​n−s.
(39)
The omitted integers are all greater than P, so the difference from ζ(s) has modulus at most ∑n>P​n−σ→0. Thus
ζ(s)=p∏​(1−p−s)−1(Res>1).​
(40)
This defines the infinite Euler product as the limit of finite products. Its absolute convergence also follows from ∑p​p−σ<∞, with log(1−p−s)−1=p−s+O(p−2σ) for sufficiently large p.

ζ(s)−s−11​=1−s∫1∞​{x}x−s−1dx(Res>0).​

The compactness theorem states that a set of first-order sentences has a model if every finite subset has a model. The Upward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem says that an infinite structure M in a language L has an elementary extension of every prescribed infinite cardinality κ≥max(∣M∣,∣L∣,ℵ0​).
Add constants ca​ for all a∈M and the elementary diagram of a structure of M: every sentence with these constants true in M. Add κ further constants di​ and sentences di​=dj​ for i=j. Any finite subset is satisfiable in M, by choosing the finitely many new constants distinctly, since M is infinite. Compactness gives a model containing an elementary copy of M and at least κ elements.
For the exact cardinality, start with that copy and all the di​, a set of cardinality κ. For every existential formula with parameters from this set that holds in the large model, choose one witness. Also close under the language's functions. Repeat countably many times. At each stage there are at most κ formulas and finite parameter tuples, so the union still has cardinality κ. Every existential formula true in the large model with parameters in the union has a witness in the union; an induction on formulas proves that this substructure is elementary. This establishes the exact-size statement without assuming an unproved downward theorem.
A dense total order with a<b is not a well-order: the nonempty set {x:a<x} has no least element, since density supplies a point strictly between a and any proposed least element.
In the strict-order language, the required axioms are
∀x ¬(x<x),∀x,y,z ((x<y∧y<z)⇒x<z),
(77)
∀x,y (x=y∨x<y∨y<x),∀x,y (x<y⇒∃z (x<z∧z<y)).
(78)
These axiomatize dense total orders, allowing endpoints. If more than one point is required, add ∃x∃y (x<y). For a non-strict poset language replace x<y by x≤y∧x=y.
Dense total orders are first-order axiomatizable.​

The Turán graph Tr​(n) is the complete r-partite graph whose vertex-class sizes differ by at most one; empty classes are allowed when r>n. Its edge count is tr​(n)=21​(n2−∑i=1r​ni2​). Turan theorem states that every n-vertex graph containing no Kr+1​ has at most tr​(n) edges.
Here is a symmetrization proof, including the equality case. Let G be any Kr+1​-free graph maximizing the edge count. If nonadjacent u,v have unequal degrees, replace the lower-degree vertex by a twin of the higher-degree vertex: this increases edges and cannot create a forbidden clique, since any new clique containing the twin corresponds to an old clique containing its model. Thus all nonadjacent pairs have equal degrees.
If such u,v had distinct neighbourhoods, choose w∈N(u)∖N(v) (their equal degrees ensure such a vertex exists), and clone v onto u. The new graph has the same maximum number of edges and is still clique-free. Originally w and v were nonadjacent, so d(w)=d(v). After cloning, w loses precisely its edge to u, while v keeps its degree. They remain nonadjacent but now have different degrees, contradicting the preceding necessary property of every extremal graph. Hence nonadjacent vertices have identical neighbourhoods.
Nonadjacency together with equality is therefore an equivalence relation, making G complete multipartite. It has at most r classes, otherwise choosing one vertex from each of r+1 classes gives a clique. For fixed total size, ∑ni2​ is minimized by r classes balanced as equally as possible: splitting a nontrivial class when fewer than r classes are used adds edges, and moving a vertex from a class of size at least two greater than another also adds edges. Thus every extremal graph is Tr​(n), up to isomorphism. This proves both the bound and its equality characterization. In particular
ex(K3​;n)=t2​(n)=⌊n2/4⌋.​
(84)
For the bipartite assertion, take a maximum matching in a graph of a edges. No edge joins two unmatched vertices. Let U be its 2a endpoints. For each matched pair uv, both u and v cannot have neighbours outside U: those two neighbours lie in opposite vertex classes and would replace uv by two disjoint edges, increasing the matching. Thus at most n−a edges from this pair lead outside U, giving ∣F∣≤a(n−a). There are at most a2 edges within U. Consequently
e(G)≤a2+a(n−a)=an.
(85)
If e(G)>(k−1)n, necessarily a≥k.
Finally let A,B,C be the three classes of the triangle-free graph. If m=e(A,B)=0, the desired bound is immediate. Otherwise set k=⌈m/n⌉. The preceding result gives k disjoint AB edges. For each edge uv, the C-neighbourhoods of its endpoints are disjoint, or there would be a triangle, so dC​(u)+dC​(v)≤n. The other 2(n−k) vertices of A∪B each have at most n neighbours in C. Hence
e(A,C)+e(B,C)≤kn+2(n−k)n=2n2−kn.
(86)
Since m≤kn,
e(H)≤2n2.​

The spectrum of a bounded operator is σ(T)={λ∈C:T−λI has no bounded everywhere-defined inverse}. Initially define T on finite linear combinations of the orthonormal basis. The bilateral shift operator Sen​=en+1​ preserves the Hilbert space norm and extends to a unitary operator on H; its inverse is S∗en​=en−1​. Thus T=S+S∗ extends uniquely by density, is bounded with norm at most two, and is self-adjoint.
For vN​=(2N+1)−1/2∑n=−NN​en​, ∥vN​∥=1 and the only nonzero coefficients of (T−2I)vN​ occur at −N−1,−N,N,N+1. Hence

It follows that ∥TvN​∥→2, proving ∥T∥=2​. Also 2∈σ(T)​: a bounded inverse of T−2I would give 1≤∥(T−2I)−1∥∥(T−2I)vN​∥→0. Thus two belongs to the approximate point spectrum.
An eigenvector x=∑xn​en​ would satisfy λxn​=xn−1​+xn+1​. Self-adjointness and the norm bound force λ∈[−2,2]. If ∣λ∣<2, write λ=2cosθ with 0<θ<π; the general complex solution of the linear recurrence relation is

At λ=±2, the general solution is (A+Bn)(±1)n, again square summable only when zero. This also covers λ=0 through θ=π/2. Thus T has no eigenvectors​.
Finally the bounded sequence e3j​ has images Te3j​=e3j−1​+e3j+1​ with pairwise disjoint supports. Distinct images have distance two, so no subsequence converges. Hence T is not compact​.

The Monodromy theorem states that if a holomorphic germ can be analytically continued along every path in a domain, its continuations along paths homotopic with fixed endpoints coincide. In a simply connected domain this gives a single-valued holomorphic function on the whole domain.
Write ζj​=e2πij/n. Remove the radial rays Rj​={tζj​:t≥1} and set U=C∖⋃j​Rj​. This is an open star-shaped domain containing zero, hence simply connected, and h=zn−1 never vanishes there. Locally its logarithm continues along all paths in U, so monodromy gives a holomorphic logarithm L and
h1/r=eL/ron U.​
(104)
Equivalently, integrate h′/h on the simply connected domain and choose the additive constant to obtain eL=h.
Take r copies of the slit domain, labeled by j∈Z/rZ, carrying values e(L+2πij)/r. Across each cut identify banks so that a positive loop around its simple zero increments the sheet index by one. This cyclic gluing produces the unbranched Riemann surface over C∖Z, on which wr=zn−1 is single valued. Completing each finite puncture gives local coordinate w, with
z−ζj​=nζjn−1​wr​+O(w2r).
(105)
There is one ramification point of index r over each of the n roots of unity.
At infinity a loop around all n zeros acts on sheet labels by j↦j+n(modr). With d=gcd(n,r) this permutation has d cycles, each of length r/d. In the compactification there are therefore d points over infinity, each with ramification index r/d. Infinity is unbranched precisely when d=r, namely when r∣n. Counting branch values in the base sphere,
#{branch values of π}=n⟺r∣n;otherwise it is n+1.​
(106)
If “branch points” denotes ramification points upstairs instead, the count is n or n+d respectively, with exactly the same stated equivalence.

With the convention that the shape operator is Ap​=−dNp​, the second fundamental form is IIp​(v,w)=⟨Ap​v,w⟩ and the normal curvature in a nonzero direction w is kn​(w)=II(w,w)/⟨w,w⟩. The two principal curvatures are the real eigenvalues k1​,k2​ of this self-adjoint operator; the mean curvature is H=(k1​+k2​)/2.
For directions successively spaced around the tangent plane, write their angles to a principal direction as θj​=θ0​+(j−1)π/m. The Euler formula for normal curvature gives

Put a=ℏ/2. Operators on distinct tensor product factors commute. Acting with σx​⊗σy​⊗σy​ on ∣↑↑↑⟩ gives −∣↓↓↓⟩, while acting on ∣↓↓↓⟩ gives −∣↑↑↑⟩. Therefore their difference is an eigenvector with eigenvalue +1. The same computation applies to the permutations yxy and yyx. The product xxx flips the two basis tensors without a phase and so sends their difference to its negative.
Restoring the three factors of a, the GHZ state has
sx(1)​sy(2)​sy(3)​: +a3,sy(1)​sx(2)​sy(3)​: +a3,sy(1)​sy(2)​sx(3)​: +a3,sx(1)​sx(2)​sx(3)​: −a3.​

A putative simultaneous assignment of classical values sx(i)​,sy(i)​∈{±a} reproducing the first three certain quantum outcomes must obey, almost surely,
sx(1)​sy(2)​sy(3)​=sy(1)​sx(2)​sy(3)​=sy(1)​sy(2)​sx(3)​=a3.
(178)
Multiply the three equalities. Each y value occurs twice and its square is a2, leaving a6sx(1)​sx(2)​sx(3)​=a9. Thus
sx(1)​sx(2)​sx(3)​=+a3,​
(179)
contrary to the quantum prediction −a3.
This is the GHZ theorem against predetermined local measurement values. Experimentally prepare many copies of the three-spin state and choose independently among the four measurement settings on separated subsystems. The three mixed correlations force the classical prediction for the fourth, whereas quantum mechanics predicts the opposite sign. Since sx​,sy​ on the same subsystem do not commute, the four settings are measured on separate copies; the classical contradiction relies precisely on the common assignment of values across settings.

Bloch theorem states that energy eigenfunctions in a Bravais lattice potential may be chosen as
ψnk​(r)=eik⋅runk​(r),unk​(r+l)=unk​(r).​
(180)
The wavevector is defined modulo a reciprocal lattice vector, so one can restrict it to the first Brillouin zone. This follows because lattice translations commute with the Hamiltonian and have simultaneous eigenvalues eik⋅l.
In one dimension write V(x)=∑G​VG​eiGx with G=2πj/a and expand a Bloch state as ψk​=∑G​cG​ei(k+G)x. The Schrödinger equation becomes
[2mℏ2(k+G)2​−E]cG​+∑G′​VG−G′​cG′​=0.
(181)
For zero potential, the parabolas EG0​(k)=ℏ2(k+G)2/(2m) fold into the Brillouin zone. A weak potential shifts a nondegenerate level by V0​ at first order, with second-order correction ∑G=0​∣VG​∣2/(E00​−EG0​) where the denominators stay away from zero. This expansion fails near crossings, where degenerate perturbation theory is required.
At the first zone boundary, put G=2π/a and k=G/2+q. The nearly degenerate waves with momenta ℏk and ℏ(k−G) are coupled by VG​. Retaining their two-dimensional subspace gives
Heff​=(ϵk​+V0​VG∗​​VG​ϵk−G​+V0​​),ϵp​=2mℏ2p2​.
(182)
Diagonalizing produces
E±​(q)=V0​+2mℏ2​(4G2​+q2)±(2mℏ2Gq​)2+∣VG​∣2​.​
(183)
At q=0 there is a gap ΔE=2∣VG​∣​: the two standing-wave combinations sample the periodic potential differently. Similar Bragg degeneracies occur at k=jπ/a, with gaps controlled to first order by the corresponding Fourier components. If that component vanishes, a gap need not open at first order. Between the gaps the continuous energy eigenvalues form energy bands, periodically represented in the reduced-zone scheme. For the first zone edge, the curvature of the upper and lower branches gives a minimum and a maximum respectively for a sufficiently weak nonzero potential, so the avoided crossing is a genuine local forbidden energy interval.
At zero temperature electrons occupy states up to the Fermi energy. The Fermi surface is the set En​(k)=EF​ separating occupied from unoccupied states within partially filled bands (Fermi points in one dimension). A partially filled band supplies arbitrarily nearby empty states, allowing occupations to respond to a weak electric field and conduct. Completely filled bands give no net current from such a redistribution; if the next empty band is separated by a positive band gap, the system is a band insulator. Band overlap can instead yield a metal even at an integer band filling. At finite temperature an insulator can conduct through thermally excited electrons and holes.

Assume A>0 and α>0, so the excitation energy increases with momentum and vanishes in the ground state. With one internal state, the number of states in a spherical momentum shell is V4πk2dk/(2π)3. Since k=(ϵ/A)1/α/ℏ,
g(ϵ)dϵ=2π2αℏ3A3/αV​ϵ3/α−1dϵ.​
(184)
An internal degeneracy multiplies this density of states by its degeneracy factor.
The Bose-Einstein distribution is nˉ(ϵ)=[e(ϵ−μ)/(kB​T)−1]−1. For a finite nonnegative occupation of the zero-energy state, its denominator must be positive, requiring μ<0. At Bose-Einstein condensation the thermodynamic-limit chemical potential approaches 0 from below, and the ground state must be counted separately; therefore “μ<0” is a finite-system condition, while the condensed limit has μ=0.
In a box whose shape is fixed, each momentum quantum number scales as V−1/3, so each energy level scales as V−α/3. Differentiating the grand potential Ω=kB​T∑j​log(1−e−(ϵj​−μ)/(kB​T)) at fixed T,μ gives
p=−(∂V∂Ω​)T,μ​=∑j​nˉj​3Vαϵj​​,pV=3α​Etotal​.​
(185)
The zero-energy condensate contributes neither pressure nor kinetic energy.
The number outside the ground state is
Nex​=2π2αℏ3A3/αV​∫0∞​e(ϵ−μ)/(kB​T)−1ϵ3/α−1​dϵ.​
(186)
At μ↑0, its low-energy integrand is proportional to ϵ3/α−2. The integral is finite precisely when 3/α>1, so
a finite-density condensate is possible for 0<α<3.​
(187)
For these exponents, the maximum excited population is
Nexmax​=2π2αℏ3A3/αVΓ(3/α)ζ(3/α)​(kB​T)3/α.
(188)
This follows by expanding the Bose denominator in positive exponentials and integrating each term. It tends to zero as T↓0, forcing excess particles into the ground state at fixed nonzero total number. At α=3 the divergence is logarithmic; for α>3 it is stronger, so there is no positive-temperature thermodynamic-limit condensation of this homogeneous gas.
Photons have α=1 and two polarizations, but in ordinary blackbody equilibrium their number is not conserved and μ=0 at every temperature. Cooling reduces their number rather than forcing an excess into a ground state, so an ordinary equilibrium photon gas does not condense. Systems imposing an effective photon-number constraint and an appropriate confined spectrum are different from the unconstrained photon gas considered here.

Use SI units, xa=(ct,x) and metric signature (+,−,−,−). The four-current is ja=(cρ,j). Charge density and current transform together under Lorentz transformations, and the continuity equation becomes
∂a​ja=∂t​ρ+∇⋅j=0.​
(189)
With the four-potential Aa=(φ/c,A), the Lorenz gauge ∂a​Aa=0 converts Maxwell equations to □Aa=μ0​ja, where □=c−2∂t2​−∇2. Choosing no incoming homogeneous radiation, the retarded electromagnetic potential is
Aa(x,t)=4πμ0​​∫∣x−x′∣ja(x′,t−∣x−x′∣/c)​d3x′.​
(190)
Current conservation ensures this solution obeys the Lorenz gauge; a homogeneous solution may be added when additional field boundary data are specified.
For a thin loop, let R=∣x∣, R=x/R and tR​=t−R/c. Then
A=4πμ0​​∮∣x−x′∣I(t−∣x−x′∣/c)​dℓ′.

In the small-loop magnetic-dipole approximation, expand ∣x−x′∣=R−R⋅x′+⋯. The constant term integrates to zero because ∮dℓ′=0. The first nonzero term is
4πμ0​​[R2I(tR​)​+cRI˙(tR​)​]∮(R⋅x′)dℓ′.
(192)
For the oriented circular loop the last integral is πr2n×R. Thus with magnetic dipole moment m(t)=πr2I(t)n,
A(x,t)=4μ0​I0​r2​[R2sin(ωtR​)​+cRωcos(ωtR​)​]n×R.​
(193)
The R−2 term is the near dipole potential and the R−1 term its radiation potential. This is the leading small-r result at fixed R,ω; besides r/R≪1, the expansion of the retarded current requires ωr/c≪1.
If only r/R≪1 is imposed and the loop need not be small compared with a wavelength, keep the retarded phase around the loop. For fixed r,ω and R→∞, the leading far-field expression is instead
A=2Rμ0​I0​r​J1​(cωr​sinθ)cos(ωtR​)sinθn×R​+O(R−2),

where cosθ=n⋅R and J1​ is the Bessel function of the first kind. Integrating the sinusoidal phase on a circle gives this Bessel factor; J1​(z)∼z/2 recovers the radiation part of the boxed dipole result.

A plane wave in the rest frame of the medium has phase k⋅x−Ω0​(k)t. Under the Galilean transformation x′=x−Ut, this becomes k⋅x′−[Ω0​(k)−U⋅k]t. Therefore
ω=Ω0​(k)−U⋅k,cg​=∇k​Ω0​−U.​
(203)
Here cg​ is the group velocity in the moving frame.
For acoustic waves, Ω0​=c0​∣k∣ and take U=Mc0​ex​. A steady wave has ω=0, requiring cosβ=1/M, where β is the angle of k to the flight direction. Its ray velocity is c0​k−Mc0​ex​, with backward component −c0​(M2−1)/M and transverse magnitude c0​M2−1​/M. Thus the angle θ of the ray to the backward flight direction obeys
tanθ=M2−1​1​,θ=sin−1(1/M).​
(204)
The axial symmetry gives the Mach cone behind the aircraft.
For unsteady emitted disturbances, all ray velocities lie on the sphere cg​=−U+c0​k. Since M>1, the origin lies outside this velocity sphere and its tangent cone has exactly the same semi-angle. All other rays are strictly inside the cone. Equivalently a signal emitted τ time units ago has a wavefront sphere centered at −Uτ with radius c0​τ; these spheres are enclosed by their Mach-cone envelope. Consequently the unsteady wavefield is confined to the cone's interior, with the steady envelope on its boundary.
For capillary waves put a=T/ρ​, so Ω0​=ak3/2. The positive-frequency steady condition is ak​=Ucosβ, requiring cosβ>0. Then
∇k​Ω0​=23​ak​(cosβ,sinβ),
(205)
and
cg​=U(23​cos2β−1, 23​cosβsinβ).​
(206)
Its endpoint traces the circle
(Ucgx​​+41​)2+(Ucgy​​)2=(43​)2,
(207)
since cgx​/U=−1/4+(3/4)cos2β and cgy​/U=(3/4)sin2β. As β runs through (−π/2,π/2) this traces the circle except its leftmost limiting point, corresponding to the zero-wavenumber limit. The circle surrounds the origin, so every direction except the precisely backward axis is attained by a nonzero-wavenumber steady ray; the backward direction is approached as k↓0. Thus the closure of the steady ray field extends all around the insect, with no excluded angular sector such as the acoustic Mach-cone exterior.
